subtopic_detail: Timing of ventilatory support in motor neuron disease using supine vital capacity and nocturnal symptoms
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a neurology clinic reviewing a 61-year-old man diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis fourteen months ago. He has been taking riluzole since diagnosis and attends a multidisciplinary clinic every three months.

He tells you he now sleeps 'propped up on four pillows' because lying flat makes him feel he cannot get enough air, wakes two or three times a night, and has a dull headache for the first hour after waking that clears by mid-morning. He dozes off in the afternoon, which is new.

He has wasting of both hands with fasciculations, brisk reflexes and mild dysarthria, but swallows normally and his weight is stable. Forced vital capacity is 68 per cent predicted sitting and falls to 52 per cent predicted when supine. Daytime arterial carbon dioxide tension is 44 mmHg. Overnight oximetry shows the oxygen saturation below 90 per cent for 24 per cent of the recording.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 130/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 96 per cent on room air seated, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Respiratory symptoms: Orthopnoea requiring four pillows, two to three nocturnal awakenings, morning headache clearing by mid-morning, new daytime somnolence
data_table.Lung function: Forced vital capacity 68 per cent predicted sitting, falling to 52 per cent predicted supine
data_table.Gas exchange: Daytime arterial carbon dioxide tension 44 mmHg; overnight oximetry with saturation below 90 per cent for 24 per cent of the recording
data_table.Neurological and nutritional: Wasted fasciculating hands, brisk reflexes, mild dysarthria, normal swallow, stable weight

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start riluzole and review his respiratory function again in three months
options.rationale: He has taken riluzole since diagnosis, and in any case it extends survival by a few months without altering diaphragmatic weakness or nocturnal hypoventilation. Deferring for three months allows a further substantial fall in vital capacity. (Source: MND Australia: Clinical guidance)

options.text: Arrange a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy before any other intervention
options.rationale: Gastrostomy is indicated for dysphagia with weight loss or unsafe swallowing, and his swallow is normal with a stable weight. Placing a tube once vital capacity has fallen below 50 per cent predicted also becomes substantially more hazardous, which is an argument for doing it earlier when it is genuinely needed, not for doing it now. (Source: MND Australia: Clinical guidance)

options.text: Start nocturnal oxygen by nasal prongs at 2 L/min and review him in one month
options.rationale: Oxygen alone treats the saturation without supporting ventilation and can worsen carbon dioxide retention by reducing hypoxic respiratory drive in a patient whose problem is pump failure. Supplemental oxygen is used only alongside ventilatory support or in the palliative phase. (Source: MND Australia: Clinical guidance)

options.text: Refer now for assessment and initiation of non-invasive nocturnal ventilation
options.rationale: Orthopnoea, disturbed sleep, morning headache and daytime somnolence with a supine fall in vital capacity to 52 per cent predicted and significant nocturnal desaturation indicate diaphragmatic weakness with nocturnal hypoventilation, which is the trigger for non-invasive ventilation. Started at this point it improves survival by several months and improves quality of life more than any other intervention in this disease, and a normal daytime carbon dioxide does not exclude the diagnosis because hypoventilation appears first during sleep. (Source: MND Australia: Clinical guidance)

options.text: Start morphine and a benzodiazepine for breathlessness and review in a month
options.rationale: Opioids and benzodiazepines are the mainstay of symptom control for dyspnoea in the terminal phase or when ventilation has been declined or withdrawn. Used now they would suppress an already failing respiratory drive in a man who is ambulant, eating normally and has months to years of useful function ahead. (Source: MND Australia: Clinical guidance)

explanation.summary: Respiratory failure is the usual cause of death in motor neuron disease and arises from progressive weakness of the diaphragm and accessory muscles rather than from lung pathology. Because the diaphragm is loaded most when supine, the earliest measurable abnormality is a fall in vital capacity on lying flat and the earliest symptoms are orthopnoea, fragmented sleep, morning headache and daytime sleepiness, all of which precede any daytime rise in carbon dioxide. Monitoring therefore uses seated and supine forced vital capacity, sniff nasal inspiratory pressure and overnight oximetry at each clinic visit, because a single seated measurement will miss the transition. Non-invasive ventilation started at the point of nocturnal hypoventilation prolongs survival and improves quality of life and cognition, with the benefit greatest in patients without severe bulbar involvement. Discussions about ventilation, gastrostomy and advance care planning are held early while communication is intact, and are revisited as the disease progresses.
key_points: Supine vital capacity falls before seated vital capacity because the diaphragm is loaded lying flat
Morning headache, orthopnoea and daytime somnolence indicate nocturnal hypoventilation
A normal daytime carbon dioxide does not exclude nocturnal hypoventilation
Non-invasive ventilation improves both survival and quality of life when started at this stage
Oxygen without ventilatory support can worsen carbon dioxide retention
explanation.pearls: Place a gastrostomy while forced vital capacity is still above 50 per cent predicted; beyond that point the procedure carries a markedly higher risk of respiratory complications and radiologically inserted gastrostomy under non-invasive ventilation becomes the safer route.

subtopic_detail: Choosing the initial screening test when acral and facial change suggests growth hormone excess
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 44-year-old man referred with bilateral hand numbness that wakes him at night and is worst in the thumb and index finger. He mentions in passing that he has had his wedding ring enlarged twice and has gone up two shoe sizes in five years.

His wife, who attends with him, says his jaw 'looks heavier' and produces a photograph from eight years ago that shows noticeably finer features and a smaller nose.

On examination his hands are broad with doughy soft tissue, there is an interdental gap that he says is new, and the tongue appears enlarged. Tinel sign is positive bilaterally at the wrist. Blood pressure is 158/94 mmHg on two occasions and fasting glucose is 6.6 mmol/L. He has no headache and no visual symptoms, and confrontation visual fields are full.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 158/94 mmHg on two occasions, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Examination: Broad hands with doughy soft tissue, new interdental separation, enlarged tongue, coarsened facial features against a photograph from eight years ago
data_table.Neurological: Tinel sign positive bilaterally at the wrist; confrontation visual fields full

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.text: Measure a random serum growth hormone level as the initial screening test
options.rationale: Growth hormone is secreted in pulses with a short half-life, so a random level overlaps between health and disease and a normal value cannot exclude the diagnosis. Growth hormone is measured meaningfully only during a dynamic suppression test. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary as the initial investigation
options.rationale: Imaging follows biochemical confirmation because incidental pituitary lesions are found in around 10 per cent of the population and an unconfirmed abnormality generates unnecessary surgery. Once excess secretion is proven, magnetic resonance imaging defines the adenoma and its relation to the optic chiasm. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Measure a serum insulin-like growth factor 1 as the initial screening test
options.rationale: Insulin-like growth factor 1 is produced by the liver in response to integrated growth hormone exposure and has a long half-life, so a single age-matched measurement reflects average secretion over the preceding day and is the recommended screening test. A raised result is confirmed by failure of growth hormone to suppress below 1 microgram/L during a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test, after which imaging is arranged. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Measure an early morning serum cortisol as the initial screening investigation
options.rationale: Cortisol screening addresses Cushing syndrome, which shares hypertension and impaired glucose tolerance with this presentation but produces central obesity, proximal myopathy, thin skin and striae rather than acral enlargement. Acral growth and coarsened features are not features of cortisol excess. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange a 48 hour low dose dexamethasone suppression test as the first step
options.rationale: This is a confirmatory test for cortisol excess and is used after an abnormal first-line screen such as late night salivary cortisol or 24 hour urinary free cortisol. It examines an axis that is not implicated by the clinical findings here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Acromegaly is caused in almost all cases by a growth hormone secreting pituitary adenoma, and diagnosis is typically delayed by 7 to 10 years because the changes are insidious and the patient sees themselves daily. Comparison with old photographs is one of the most useful bedside manoeuvres available. Presenting complaints are often the complications rather than the appearance: carpal tunnel syndrome, obstructive sleep apnoea, hypertension, impaired glucose tolerance or type 2 diabetes, arthropathy and cardiomyopathy. Insulin-like growth factor 1 is the screening test because it integrates pulsatile growth hormone secretion, and confirmation uses failure of growth hormone suppression during an oral glucose tolerance test, with imaging reserved for after biochemical proof. Transsphenoidal surgery is first-line treatment, with somatostatin analogues, the growth hormone receptor antagonist pegvisomant, dopamine agonists and radiotherapy used for residual disease, and mortality, which is increased mainly through cardiovascular disease, returns towards normal once growth hormone and insulin-like growth factor 1 are brought into the target range.
key_points: Insulin-like growth factor 1 is the screening test; random growth hormone is uninterpretable
Confirm with failure of growth hormone suppression during an oral glucose tolerance test
Image the pituitary only after biochemical confirmation
Compare with old photographs, since the changes are too gradual for the patient to notice
Screen for sleep apnoea, diabetes, hypertension, cardiomyopathy and colonic neoplasia
explanation.pearls: Colonoscopy is recommended at diagnosis in acromegaly and repeated according to findings and disease control, because growth hormone excess raises the risk of colonic adenomas and carcinoma independently of other factors.

subtopic_detail: Dorsal column signs with a serum cobalamin inside the reference range in a recreational inhalant user
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 24-year-old hospitality worker referred with six weeks of numbness and tingling that began in both feet and has ascended to just below both knees. He says he now has to 'watch my feet to know where they are' and stumbles badly in a dark corridor.

He eats a mixed diet including meat and dairy, has had no gastrointestinal surgery and takes no metformin or proton pump inhibitor. When asked directly about recreational drugs he tells you he inhales nitrous oxide from cream chargers, roughly a hundred bulbs a week for the past eight months.

On examination vibration sense is absent at both ankles and reduced at both knees, joint position sense is impaired at both great toes, and Romberg test is positive. Ankle reflexes are absent while both plantar responses are extensor. Power is preserved. Investigations are shown.

data_table.Neurological examination: Vibration absent at ankles and reduced at knees, impaired joint position sense at the great toes, Romberg positive, ankle reflexes absent with extensor plantar responses, power preserved
data_table.Investigations: Serum vitamin B12 210 pmol/L (150-700), haemoglobin 146 g/L (130-180), mean cell volume 92 fL (80-98), no hypersegmented neutrophils on film
data_table.Metabolites: Serum homocysteine 42 micromol/L (5-15), methylmalonic acid 1.9 micromol/L (less than 0.4)
data_table.Exposure: Nitrous oxide inhalation, approximately 100 bulbs weekly for eight months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure him that the vitamin B12 level is normal and repeat it in three months
options.rationale: Nitrous oxide irreversibly oxidises the cobalt core of cobalamin, inactivating the vitamin while leaving the serum assay, which measures total cobalamin, within the reference range. Functional deficiency is demonstrated by the raised methylmalonic acid and homocysteine, which are the appropriate tests when the level is normal but the clinical picture is not. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start oral cyanocobalamin 1000 microgram daily and review him in three months
options.rationale: High dose oral replacement is effective for dietary and even for absorptive deficiency in the absence of neurological signs, and it acts too slowly for subacute combined degeneration where the window for recovery is measured in weeks. Parenteral loading is used whenever neurological involvement is present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the spine before starting any treatment
options.rationale: Imaging may show the characteristic inverted V signal change in the dorsal columns and is useful to document severity, but the biochemical and clinical picture is already diagnostic and treatment should not wait for a scan slot. Delay while imaging is arranged converts reversible deficit into permanent disability. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start oral folic acid 5 mg daily and review his neurological signs in one month
options.rationale: Folate corrects the megaloblastic anaemia of cobalamin deficiency while allowing the neurological damage to progress unchecked, which is why folate is never given first when cobalamin deficiency is possible. His homocysteine is raised through the cobalamin dependent pathway, not from folate deficiency. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start intramuscular hydroxocobalamin now and advise him to stop the nitrous oxide
options.rationale: Dorsal column loss with a positive Romberg sign, absent ankle reflexes and extensor plantar responses is subacute combined degeneration of the cord, and parenteral hydroxocobalamin is started immediately because recovery depends on how long the deficit has been present. Cessation of nitrous oxide is equally essential, since continued exposure will inactivate each replacement dose as it is given. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Nitrous oxide inactivates cobalamin by oxidising its cobalt centre, which blocks methionine synthase and produces a functional deficiency regardless of dietary intake or absorption. The consequence is subacute combined degeneration of the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts, giving the distinctive combination of sensory ataxia and absent ankle reflexes with extensor plantar responses, and a peripheral neuropathy often coexists. Serum cobalamin is frequently within the reference range because the assay measures total rather than active vitamin, so methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are the tests that establish functional deficiency. Haematological changes are commonly absent, and the neurological syndrome can occur with an entirely normal blood film, so a normal full blood count is no reassurance. Treatment is immediate parenteral hydroxocobalamin with cessation of exposure, and recovery is good when treatment starts within weeks but incomplete once the deficit has been established for months.
key_points: Nitrous oxide inactivates cobalamin directly, so serum levels are often normal
Methylmalonic acid and homocysteine demonstrate functional deficiency when the level is normal
Neurological disease can occur without anaemia or macrocytosis
Sensory ataxia with absent ankle jerks and extensor plantars is the classic cord syndrome
Treat with parenteral hydroxocobalamin immediately; oral replacement is too slow
explanation.pearls: Never give folate before cobalamin when both may be deficient: correcting the megaloblastic anaemia removes the haematological signal while methylmalonic acid continues to accumulate, and the cord lesion progresses silently.

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulant choice for venous thrombosis in a patient with an unresected luminal gastrointestinal tumour
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 67-year-old man on the oncology ward. He was diagnosed six weeks ago with a locally advanced gastric adenocarcinoma and started neoadjuvant chemotherapy, and today his left calf and thigh have become swollen and painful.

His endoscopy report describes a large ulcerated antral lesion, and he has needed two units of red cells since diagnosis for a slow drop in haemoglobin attributed to tumour ooze. He has had no melaena or haematemesis this admission.

Doppler ultrasound confirms occlusive thrombus in the left femoral and popliteal veins. His platelet count is 120 x10^9/L, creatinine clearance is 78 mL/min and liver function is within normal limits. He is taking no antiplatelet drugs and has a central venous access device in the right arm.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9°C
data_table.Imaging: Doppler ultrasound shows occlusive thrombus in the left femoral and popliteal veins
data_table.Tumour: Large ulcerated gastric antral adenocarcinoma, unresected, on neoadjuvant chemotherapy
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 120 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine clearance 78 mL/min, liver function within normal limits, haemoglobin 98 g/L (130-180) after two units of red cells
data_table.Other: No antiplatelet drugs; central venous access device in the right arm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation?

options.text: Start oral apixaban at a treatment dose and continue while the cancer is active
options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants are a reasonable choice for most cancer associated thrombosis and apixaban has the lowest bleeding signal of the class, but the trials consistently show excess major bleeding in patients with unresected luminal gastrointestinal tumours. An ulcerated antral lesion that is already bleeding is the specific situation in which the oral agents are avoided. (Source: eviQ: Cancer associated thrombosis)

options.text: Start subcutaneous low molecular weight heparin at a treatment dose and continue
options.rationale: Low molecular weight heparin remains the preferred agent for cancer associated thrombosis when there is an unresected luminal gastrointestinal tumour, active tumour bleeding, significant thrombocytopenia or concerns about oral absorption, all of which apply here. It is continued for at least 6 months and for as long as the cancer remains active or treatment continues, with the dose reduced rather than stopped if the platelet count falls further. (Source: eviQ: Cancer associated thrombosis)

options.text: Start warfarin with heparin bridging and target a ratio of 2 to 3 thereafter
options.rationale: Warfarin performs worse than low molecular weight heparin in cancer, with higher recurrence and bleeding rates, because chemotherapy, vomiting, altered nutrition and drug interactions make the international normalised ratio unstable. It is used when neither heparin nor an oral agent is feasible. (Source: eviQ: Cancer associated thrombosis)

options.text: Insert a retrievable inferior vena cava filter and withhold anticoagulation
options.rationale: A filter is reserved for patients in whom anticoagulation is absolutely contraindicated, such as active uncontrolled haemorrhage or recent intracranial bleeding, and he has had no overt bleeding this admission. Filters prevent pulmonary embolism but increase recurrent deep vein thrombosis and do not treat the existing clot. (Source: eviQ: Cancer associated thrombosis)

options.text: Start oral rivaroxaban at a treatment dose and continue for three months only
options.rationale: Rivaroxaban carries the clearest excess of gastrointestinal bleeding of the oral agents in cancer trials, which is the wrong profile for an ulcerated gastric tumour. Three months is also too short, since anticoagulation continues while the malignancy is active. (Source: eviQ: Cancer associated thrombosis)

explanation.summary: Venous thromboembolism is several times more common in people with cancer than in the general population, and it is the second commonest cause of death in patients receiving chemotherapy. Risk is driven by tumour type, with pancreatic, gastric, brain, lung and haematological malignancies at the top, and by the presence of a central venous access device, recent surgery, immobility and certain chemotherapy and antiangiogenic agents. The treatment landscape shifted with trials showing direct oral anticoagulants are at least as effective as low molecular weight heparin, so they are now first choice for many patients, but the same trials identified a consistent excess of gastrointestinal and genitourinary bleeding in patients with unresected luminal tumours at those sites. Low molecular weight heparin therefore retains a clear place where mucosal bleeding risk is high, where absorption is unreliable from vomiting or gastrointestinal resection, and where drug interactions with anticancer therapy are a concern. Anticoagulation continues for a minimum of 6 months and indefinitely while the cancer remains active, with the platelet count guiding dose reduction rather than cessation.
key_points: Direct oral anticoagulants are first choice for many cancer associated thromboses
Avoid them with unresected luminal gastrointestinal or genitourinary tumours because of bleeding
Low molecular weight heparin is preferred when absorption or mucosal bleeding is a concern
Continue for at least 6 months and while the cancer remains active
Reduce the heparin dose rather than stopping it when the platelet count falls
explanation.pearls: Anticoagulate catheter associated upper limb thrombosis and keep the line in place if it is functioning and still needed; removal is required only for infection, malfunction or persistent symptoms despite anticoagulation.

subtopic_detail: High anion gap acidosis with a raised osmolar gap and urinary crystals in a patient with no visual symptoms
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar receiving a 47-year-old man found drowsy on his garage floor by his brother, who says he drinks heavily and has been low since losing his job. He last ate yesterday morning.

He opens his eyes to voice, is confused and is breathing deeply and rapidly. He has vomited twice since arrival. He tells you his vision is completely normal and reads the wall clock across the room without difficulty, and his pupils are 4 mm and briskly reactive with normal fundi.

His brother brings in a partly empty 2 litre container of engine coolant from beside him and also a bottle of methylated spirits, and does not know whether either was opened today. Point of care glucose is 5.4 mmol/L. Investigations are shown. Urine microscopy reports abundant envelope shaped crystals and the urine fluoresces under a Wood lamp.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 34/min and deep, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.1°C
data_table.Arterial blood gas: pH 7.06, arterial carbon dioxide tension 18 mmHg, bicarbonate 7 mmol/L (22-32), lactate 2.1 mmol/L (0.5-2.2)
data_table.Biochemistry: Sodium 141 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), chloride 102 mmol/L (95-110), urea 8.2 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), creatinine 198 micromol/L (60-110), glucose 5.4 mmol/L, serum ketones 0.2 mmol/L (less than 0.6)
data_table.Osmolality: Measured serum osmolality 340 mOsm/kg (275-295); calculated osmolarity 302 mOsm/L
data_table.Urine and vision: Abundant envelope shaped crystals on microscopy, urine fluoresces under a Wood lamp; visual acuity normal, pupils 4 mm and briskly reactive, fundi normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give fomepizole now and arrange urgent haemodialysis with the renal team
options.rationale: An anion gap of 32 with an osmolar gap of 38, an undetectable ethanol, calcium oxalate crystalluria and fluorescent urine identifies ethylene glycol rather than methanol, and preserved vision with normal fundi argues against the methanol optic neuropathy. Fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase and stops further conversion to glycolic and oxalic acid, while haemodialysis is indicated here by a pH of 7.06 with acute kidney injury and removes both the parent alcohol and the accumulated metabolites. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate alone and repeat the blood gas in an hour
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is a useful adjunct that reduces tissue distribution of the acid metabolites and is given alongside definitive therapy, but on its own it does nothing to stop ongoing metabolite production. Buffering a toxic alcohol poisoning while the parent compound continues to be converted is treating the number rather than the poisoning. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give intravenous thiamine and dextrose and repeat the blood gas in an hour
options.rationale: Thiamine and glucose are given to every unwell person who drinks heavily and are entirely appropriate, but alcoholic ketoacidosis has been excluded by serum ketones of 0.2 mmol/L and cannot explain an osmolar gap of 38. Relying on this alone would allow renal failure and death from the acidosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give oral activated charcoal 50 g and observe him in the short stay unit
options.rationale: Charcoal binds alcohols poorly, the ingestion is clearly hours old given the established metabolic acidosis and renal injury, and administering it to a confused vomiting patient risks aspiration. Decontamination has no role in toxic alcohol poisoning. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give intravenous N-acetylcysteine and arrange urgent liver function testing
options.rationale: Acetylcysteine treats paracetamol poisoning, which produces hepatic injury with transaminase rise rather than an early high anion gap acidosis with an osmolar gap. Massive paracetamol ingestion can cause a lactic acidosis, but the lactate here is 2.1 mmol/L. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Toxic alcohol poisoning is suspected whenever a high anion gap metabolic acidosis is accompanied by a raised osmolar gap, calculated as measured osmolality minus calculated osmolarity with a normal value below about 10. The gap is largest early, when the parent alcohol is still present, and falls as it is metabolised while the anion gap rises, so a normal osmolar gap late in the course does not exclude the diagnosis. Ethylene glycol and methanol are separated clinically by the target organ: ethylene glycol produces calcium oxalate crystalluria, hypocalcaemia and acute kidney injury, while methanol produces blurred vision, central scotomata and a hyperaemic optic disc from formic acid toxicity to the optic nerve. Treatment for both is blockade of alcohol dehydrogenase with fomepizole, or with an ethanol infusion where fomepizole is not immediately available, combined with bicarbonate and cofactor therapy, thiamine and pyridoxine for ethylene glycol and folinic acid for methanol. Haemodialysis is added for severe acidosis, end organ injury or a high measured concentration, and it clears both the parent alcohol and its acid metabolites.
key_points: A high anion gap acidosis with an osmolar gap above 10 suggests toxic alcohol ingestion
The osmolar gap falls and the anion gap rises as the parent alcohol is metabolised
Oxalate crystalluria and renal injury indicate ethylene glycol; visual loss indicates methanol
Alcohol dehydrogenase blockade with fomepizole or ethanol stops metabolite production
Dialyse for severe acidosis, end organ injury or a high measured concentration
explanation.pearls: Sodium fluorescein is added to many automotive coolants, which is why the urine can fluoresce under a Wood lamp in ethylene glycol ingestion; the finding supports the diagnosis when positive but is too unreliable to exclude it when negative.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Ethylene glycol poisoning
